prompt: How does Microsoft's bandwidth page bill data coming into Azure from the internet?
hint: Think of why an account fills cheaply and empties expensively.

choices.text: Per GB, at the same rate as data leaving
choices.why: Leaving is charged; arriving is not.

choices.text: Free, though the writes are billed
choices.why: Right. Inbound bytes are free and inbound requests are not.

choices.text: Per GB, but only for accounts on geo-redundant replication
choices.why: Geo-replication is a transfer to the paired region, a different line.

choices.text: Per GB, at a lower rate than data leaving
choices.why: There is no inbound rate at all.

prompt: Reading 1 GB from the cool tier is billed on which meters?
hint: Hot pays one of them; cool pays a second on the same read.

choices.text: Read operations only, the same as hot
choices.why: Cool adds a charge per GB read back.

choices.text: Data retrieval only, since read operations are a charge of the hot tier
choices.why: Every tier charges for operations; cool charges more for each.

choices.text: Read operations, and data retrieval per GB
choices.why: Right: two charges on the same read.

choices.text: Bandwidth, because the bytes leave the tier
choices.why: Bandwidth is bytes leaving the region, not a tier.

prompt: At an illustrative 0.02 USD per GB-month and 0.004 USD per 10,000 read operations, how many reads cost the same as keeping 1 GB in hot for a month?
hint: Divide the two prices, then multiply by the 10,000 the read price is quoted for.

prompt: On Microsoft's sheet, which class of operation is a `List Blobs` request?
hint: Listing has a line of its own.

choices.text: A read operation, since a listing just reads names
choices.why: It reads, and it is still not priced like a read.

choices.text: None: listing is free
choices.why: Only inbound bytes are free.

choices.text: List and create container operations
choices.why: Right, a line of its own, not priced like a read.

choices.text: A charge per GB of names returned
choices.why: An operation is priced per operation, whatever it returns.

prompt: `count.py` wrote 6,000 taps as a blob each, then the same taps as one blob. How many `Put Blob` requests did each take?
hint: Read the second and third lines of its output.

choices.why: Right: same bytes, six thousand times the writes.

choices.text: 1 and 1, because the library batches small writes into one request
choices.why: Nothing batched them; every upload_blob was a request.

choices.text: 6,000 and 6,000, since a request carries one line
choices.why: The one blob of lines went in a single request.

choices.text: 6,000 and 2, the second as two blocks
choices.why: A blob that small is one Put Blob; blocks start above 64 MiB.

prompt: A container holds 12,500 blobs under one prefix. How many `List Blobs` requests does listing all their names take?
hint: One page holds at most 5,000 names.

prompt: Uploading 80 MiB with the library's defaults took 21 requests. Why?
hint: Compare it with the 64 MiB upload in the figure.

choices.text: Azure refuses any single request larger than 4 MiB
choices.why: A blob of 64 MiB went in one Put Blob.

choices.text: Above 64 MiB the library sends 20 blocks of 4 MiB and one list that commits them
choices.why: Right: max_single_put_size and max_block_size at their defaults.

choices.text: Azurite splits large blobs, where Azure takes them whole
choices.why: The splitting is the client's; the same program would send the same requests to Azure.

choices.text: One request per 4 MiB is how the bill counts, and the hook reports the bill
choices.why: The hook counts requests leaving the program; it knows nothing of a bill.

prompt: A dashboard reads 6,000 small tap blobs every morning. Which change cuts the number of operations it sends?
hint: No setting of the client changes how the data was cut up.

choices.text: Raising `max_single_get_size`
choices.why: Each blob is already one Get Blob; the size only matters above 32 MiB.

choices.text: Reading on eight threads instead of one
choices.why: Threads make it quicker; the count is the same.

choices.text: Writing the taps as one blob per day
choices.why: Right: one Get Blob instead of 6,000.

choices.text: Listing with 10,000 names a page
choices.why: A page holds at most 5,000, and the listing was not the cost.

prompt: `count.py` sees every request because it passes its function to the client as the option ___.
hint: It is called just before each request is sent.

prompt: In `costs.py`, why is the cool line dearer than the hot one for the same taps?
hint: The taps are read every morning.

choices.text: Cool's minimum of 30 days is charged again on every blob each month
choices.why: The taps stay all month; no early deletion happens.

choices.text: Cool charges more per operation, and per GB read
choices.why: Right: storage halves and everything touched grows.

choices.text: Cool blobs must be rehydrated before they can be read
choices.why: That is archive; a cool blob is read directly.

choices.text: Cool stores each blob as 64 KB
choices.why: Nothing in the program rounds a blob up.

prompt: At an illustrative 0.05 USD per 10,000 write operations, what does writing 2,000,000 blobs cost, in USD?
hint: Two hundred times ten thousand.

prompt: Which of these produce many small blobs? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section names three sources.

choices.text: A stream writer saving whatever arrived in the last few seconds
choices.why: Yes: a file per flush.

choices.text: A folder per hour per customer
choices.why: Yes: partitions too fine for the data.

choices.text: One blob per app event
choices.why: Yes: convenient to write and ruinous to read.

choices.text: A nightly job merging the day into 64 MiB files
choices.why: That is the cure, not the cause.

prompt: `costs.py` reads each 64 MiB file in nine requests. Where does the nine come from?
hint: `count.py` read 80 MiB in thirteen.

choices.text: Azure caps a single read at 8 MiB, so 64 MiB takes eight reads and a check
choices.why: The library's first read took 32 MiB.

choices.text: One `List Blobs` to find the file, then eight reads of 8 MiB
choices.why: The listing is counted apart, once a day.

choices.text: The first 32 MiB in one request, then 8 ranges of 4 MiB
The file was written in nine blocks, and is read back the same way
choices.why: A 64 MiB blob goes up in one Put Blob, and reading does not follow the blocks.

prompt: At an illustrative 0.10 USD per GB past the free 100 GB of the month, what does sending 5,120 GB to the internet in one month cost, in USD?
hint: Take the free part off first.

prompt: For the images behind a content delivery network, why does `costs.py` print dashes for transfer and total?
hint: Somebody still delivers the bytes to the viewers.

choices.text: Transfer behind a delivery network is free
choices.why: The network charges for delivery; it is just not in this program.

choices.text: The account sends nothing once the network is in front
choices.why: One download in twenty still reaches the account.

choices.text: Azurite has no delivery network, so the line was never run
choices.why: `costs.py` runs no emulator; it is arithmetic.

choices.text: The network's price is not in the program
choices.why: Right, and so is whether the leg from the account to it is charged.

prompt: A partner copies 5 TB out of Quitanda's account into another region, with a SAS token Quitanda issued. Whose bill carries the transfer?
hint: Look for a setting that moves the bill.

choices.text: Quitanda's: nothing in Blob Storage bills the reader
choices.why: Right: the owner pays, whoever reads.

choices.text: The partner's, because a SAS token identifies who is reading
choices.why: A SAS token grants access; it says nothing about billing.

choices.text: Nobody's: reads made with a SAS token are free
choices.why: Operations and transfer are billed however the request was authorised.

choices.text: The partner's, as long as the token expires within the day
choices.why: Expiry limits how long the door is open, not who pays.

prompt: A nightly job in a private subnet with a NAT gateway reads 2 TB a month from an account in the same region. Which change removes the charge per GB at no cost?
hint: One of the two ways past the gateway is free.

choices.text: A private endpoint for the account
choices.why: It removes the gateway's charge and adds its own, per GB in both directions.

choices.text: A service endpoint for `Microsoft.Storage` on the subnet
choices.why: Right: the traffic leaves the gateway and nothing replaces the charge.

choices.text: Moving the account from ZRS to LRS
choices.why: Redundancy changes capacity, not what the gateway processes.

choices.text: Putting a content delivery network in front of the account
choices.why: That is for viewers on the internet, not a job in the same region.

prompt: Which line does an account on GRS pay that the same account on ZRS does not?
hint: Where do the extra copies go?

choices.text: Data retrieval, per GB read back
choices.why: Retrieval belongs to the cooler tiers.

choices.text: A charge for traffic between ZRS's three zones
choices.why: ZRS's copies are paid in its capacity price.

choices.text: Geo-replication data transfer, per GB
choices.why: Right: every write is copied to the paired region.

choices.text: None at all: the two cost the same
choices.why: The second region is a transfer, and it is billed.

prompt: Match each route of a byte with what Microsoft's pricing pages charge for it.
hint: One of them is free, and one charge on the right belongs to no route.

pairs.left: Same region, through a service endpoint
Same region, through a NAT gateway
pairs.right: per GB processed, plus an hourly price

pairs.left: To the paired region, on GRS

pairs.right: first 100 GB a month free, then per GB
